extracted.intended_audience: jurors, judges, and litigators in U.S. patent infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for claim construction and various types of patent infringement (literal, means/step-plus-function, doctrine of equivalents, inducement, contributory infringement, §271(f) supply/import theories). Provides elements, burdens, and limiting doctrines for jury findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the court in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The court determines the meaning of claim terms and provides definitions of certain claim terms; jurors must accept the court’s definitions as correct and apply them to decide issues such as infringement and validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The law says that it is my role to define the terms of the claims and it is your role to apply my definitions to the issues that you are asked to decide in this case... You must accept my definitions of these words in the claims as being correct. It is your job to take these definitions and apply them to the issues that you are deciding, including the issues of infringement and validity." (Also: when the court has not defined a term, jurors should apply the common meaning.)

rubrics_metrics.name: How a claim defines what it covers
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim sets forth, in words, a set of requirements in a single sentence; if a device or method satisfies each of these requirements, then it is covered by the claim. Coverage is assessed claim-by-claim using claim elements/limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Each claim sets forth its requirements in a single sentence. If a device or a method satisfies each of these requirements, then it is covered by the claim... The coverage of a patent is assessed claim-by-claim... a claim covers a product or process where each of the claim elements or limitations is present in that product or process."

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase meanings (comprising/consisting of/consisting essentially of)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional words in claims affect scope: 'comprising' is open-ended and allows additional elements; 'consisting of' is closed (claims what follows and nothing else); 'consisting essentially of' is intermediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited and illustrative language: Invitrogen/ Biocrest ("comprising" open-ended); Vehicular Techs./Titan Wheel ("consisting of" = "I claim what follows and nothing else"); CIAS/AK Steel ("consisting essentially of" is middle ground).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim sets forth all requirements necessary to be covered; a dependent claim refers to another claim and incorporates its requirements while adding additional ones; to determine a dependent claim's coverage you must look at both the dependent claim and the claim(s) it refers to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "An 'independent claim' sets forth all of the requirements... A dependent claim ... refers to another claim for some of its requirements... A dependent claim incorporates all of the requirements of the claim(s) to which it refers. The dependent claim then adds its own additional requirements." (Note: may be helpful to submit a chart of dependencies to the jury.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation by court and use of common meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The court will explain the meaning of some claim words; jurors must accept those definitions. For terms the court has not defined, jurors should apply the common meaning, based on a person of ordinary skill in the art where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "For any words in the claim for which I have not provided you with a definition, you should apply their common meaning... You should not take my definition ... as an indication that I have a view regarding how you should decide the issues... These issues are yours to decide." Authorities: Markman; Phillips (ordinary and customary meaning tied to person of ordinary skill in the art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112, paragraph 6 (means-plus-function / step-plus-function) — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'means for [function]' (or 'step for [function]') limitation covers the structure(s) or acts described in the specification that perform the recited function and equivalents thereof; it does not cover all structures/acts that could perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "It covers a structure or a set of structures that performs that function and that is either identical or 'equivalent' to [at least one of] the [set(s) of] structure(s) described in the [ ] patent... For step-plus-function, it covers acts that perform that function and are either identical or 'equivalent' to [the described acts]." Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §112, ¶6 and cases (Allvoice, Applied Med. Res., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence test for means/step-plus-function limitations (§112 ¶6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure/action meets a §112 ¶6 limitation if it performs the identical function recited and is identical or equivalent to the structure/act(s) disclosed in the specification; equivalence is assessed as whether differences are insubstantial or whether it performs the function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, and equivalence is judged as of the time the patent issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Equivalence ... if a person having ordinary skill ... would have considered the differences ... insubstantial ... or would have found the [structure(s)/action(s)] performed the function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result... The fact that ... is known now and is 'equivalent' is not enough. ... must also have been available at the time the patent issued." Authorities: WMS Gaming, Al-Site, Omega Eng'g, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement generally — claim-by-claim and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim; there are five possible types of infringement (direct infringement, active inducement, contributory infringement, infringement through supply of components from the U.S. to another country (§271(f)), and infringement through importation of a product made abroad by a patented process). Active inducement and contributory are indirect and require someone else to have engaged in direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Infringement is assessed on a claim-by-claim basis... The five types of infringement are called: (1) direct infringement; (2) active inducement; (3) contributory infringement; (4) infringement through the supply of components from the United States to another country; and (5) infringement through importation of a product made abroad by a patented process." Burden: preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: Warner-Lambert v. Teva; Seal-Flex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof standard for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: All elements required for a type of infringement must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "In order to prove infringement, [patent holder] must prove that the requirements for one or more of these types of infringement are met by a preponderance of the evidence..." Authorities: Warner-Lambert Co. v. Teva Pharms. USA, Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — literal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove literal direct infringement, the patent holder must show by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused made, used, sold, offered for sale, or imported a product or process that meets all of the requirements of a claim during the patent term, without permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You must compare the [product or process] with each and every one of the requirements of a claim to determine whether all of the requirements of that claim are met." (If a claim element is missing, there is no literal infringement.) Authorities: MicroStrategy; Cross Med.; Netword; Moleculon Research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — literal infringement of §112 ¶6 (means/step-plus) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A product/process meets a means/step-plus-function requirement literally only if it (1) performs the identical function recited and (2) the structure/action performing it is identical or equivalent to the disclosed structure/acts; otherwise there is no literal infringement of that limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "A product or a process meets a means-plus-function requirement ... if: (1) it has [a structure or set of structures/action or set of actions] that perform(s) the identical function recited in the claim, and (2) that [structure or set of structures/action or set of actions] is either identical or 'equivalent' to [one or more of] the described [set(s) of] [structure(s)/action(s)] ... If the [product] does not perform the specific function recited in the claim, the 'means-plus-function' requirement is not met." Authorities: §112 ¶6; Omega Eng'g; Allvoice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — doctrine of equivalents (DOE) test
rubrics_metrics.description: If an accused product/process does not literally meet all claim requirements, it may still infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if each requirement is met by an equivalent element/action; equivalency is judged by whether differences are insubstantial or whether the element/action performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result, and the equivalence must have been known at the time of the alleged infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You may find that an element or step is equivalent ... if a person having ordinary skill ... would have considered the differences between them to be 'insubstantial' or would have found that the [structure or action]: (1) performs substantially the same function and (2) works in substantially the same way (3) to achieve substantially the same result... In order to prove infringement by 'equivalents,' [patent holder] must prove the equivalency ... by a preponderance of the evidence." Authorities: Graver Tank; Warner-Jenkinson; Festo; Interactive Pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prior art / hypothetical claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art may preclude DOE: if a hypothetical claim that would literally cover the accused equivalent would have been invalid as anticipated or obvious in view of the prior art, there can be no DOE for that equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two formulations given: (1) determine prior art and what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill; if a product with the allegedly equivalent feature was in prior art or would have been obvious, find no DOE; (2) use a 'hypothetical claim' broadened to cover the accused equivalent and decide whether that hypothetical claim would have been invalid for anticipation or obviousness. Authorities: Festo; cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — patent disclosure preclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not find DOE if the allegedly equivalent alternative feature was described somewhere in the patent and that product/process is not covered literally by any claim of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You may not find that a [product or process] infringes a claim under the doctrine of equivalents if you find that: (1) the allegedly 'equivalent' alternative feature(s) ... was/were described somewhere in the patent and (2) that [product or process] is not covered literally by any of the claims of the patent."

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel (argument-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: If during prosecution the applicant distinguished a claim requirement from the allegedly equivalent alternative, the patentee may be precluded from asserting DOE for that alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You may not find that a [product or process] infringes a claim under the doctrine of equivalents if you find that, during the patent application process, the applicant for the patent distinguished an unmet requirement from the allegedly 'equivalent' alternative aspect of that [product or process]."

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — prosecution history estoppel (amendment-based) — factors to overcome estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alleged amendment during prosecution is asserted to limit DOE, the patentee can still show equivalence only if at least one specified factor is met (amendment substituted broader for narrower, reason not related to patentability, unforeseeability to a person of ordinary skill at time of amendment, amendment was tangential, or other good reason such as language shortcomings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed factors jurors must find at least one of: (1) amendment substituted a broader requirement for a narrower requirement or replaced equal scope; (2) reason for amendment was not related to patentability; (3) person of ordinary skill would not have foreseen substitution of the allegedly equivalent alternative; (4) reason for amendment is tangential; or (5) other reason (e.g., language shortcomings) prevented broader claim language. If none found, estoppel precludes DOE. Authorities cited re: Festo and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents — vitiation
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged equivalent cannot be found to be equivalent if doing so would effectively eliminate or ignore an element or requirement of the claim (i.e., it would vitiate an element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You may not determine that an alternative aspect ... is equivalent to an unmet requirement of a claim if a finding of infringement under the doctrine of equivalents would effectively eliminate that requirement. Specifically, the alleged equivalent cannot eliminate or ignore an element or requirement of the claim." Authorities: Honeywell; Festo; Interactive Pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — active inducement (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Active inducement requires proof, by a preponderance of the evidence, that (1) someone else actually carried out acts that directly infringe the claim; (2) the alleged inducer took action intending to cause those infringing acts during the patent term; and (3) the alleged inducer was aware of the patent and knew the acts would constitute infringement (or acted with willful blindness to a high probability of infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "[Alleged infringer] is liable for active inducement ... only if [patent holder] proves ... that the acts are actually carried out by [another] and directly infringe ... that [alleged infringer] took action ... intending to cause the infringing acts ... and that [alleged infringer] was aware of the [ ] patent and knew that the acts, if taken, would constitute infringement..." Willful blindness language incorporated from Global-Tech. A good-faith belief that acts did not infringe or that the patent was invalid negates inducement intent. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(b); Global-Tech; DSU Med.; Lucent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement — contributory infringement (elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement requires proof, by a preponderance of the evidence, that (1) the defendant sold, offered to sell, or imported within the U.S. a component or apparatus for use in a process during the patent term; (2) the component has no substantial noninfringing use; (3) the component constitutes a material part of the invention; (4) the defendant knew of the patent and knew the component had no other substantial use and may be covered by a claim or satisfy a claim under DOE; and (5) that use directly infringes the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All listed requirements must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §271(c); Aro; Ricoh; Alloc; Mentor H/S; Hewlett-Packard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement through supply of components from U.S. for combination abroad (§271(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where §271(f)(1) or §271(f)(2) is asserted, the jury should be instructed on elements for liability for supplying components from the U.S. for combination abroad; §271(f)(1) involves 'active inducement' language (i.e., supplying or causing to be supplied components from the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should be given if patentee asserts infringement under §271(f)(1) or §271(f)(2). (Text in the chunk begins the §271(f)(1) formulation: '[Alleged infringer] is liable for §271(f)(1) infringement ... if patentee proves by a preponderance of the evidence that: [alleged infringer] supplies [or causes to be supplied] components from the United States ...'). Further elements and detailed formulation appear elsewhere in the instructions.
